rules.desc: String representations of URIs or URLs are prone to parsing and encoding errors which can lead to vulnerabilities. The System.Uri class is a safe alternative and should be preferred.

rules.title: Threads should not lock on objects with weak identity
rules.desc: Objects that can be accessed across application domain boundaries are said to have weak identity. This means that these objects can be considered shared resources outside of the domain, which can be lead to them being accessed or modified by multiple threads or concurrent parts of a program, outside of the domain.

rules.title: Pointers to unmanaged memory should not be visible
rules.desc: Pointer and unmanaged function pointer types such as IntPtr, UIntPtr, int* etc. are used to access unmanaged memory, usually in order to use C or C++ libraries. If such a pointer is not secured by making it private, internal or readonly, it can lead to a vulnerability allowing access to arbitrary locations.

rules.title: Disposable types should declare finalizers
rules.desc: This rule raises an issue when a disposable type contains fields of the following types and does not implement a finalizer:

rules.title: Collection properties should be readonly
rules.desc: A writable collection property can be replaced by a completely different collection. Making it readonly prevents that while still allowing individual members to be set. If you want to allow the replacement of the whole collection the recommended pattern is to implement a method to remove all the elements (e.g. System.Collections.List<T>.Clear) and a method to populate the collection (e.g. System.Collections.List<T>.AddRange).

rules.title: "System.Uri" arguments should be used instead of strings
rules.desc: String representations of URIs or URLs are prone to parsing and encoding errors which can lead to vulnerabilities. The System.Uri class is a safe alternative and should be preferred.

rules.title: Inherited member visibility should not be decreased
rules.desc: Decreasing the accessibility level of an inherited method that is not overridable to private will shadow the name of the base method and can lead to confusion.

rules.title: Enumeration members should not be named "Reserved"
rules.desc: If an enum member’s name contains the word "reserved" it implies it is not currently used and will be change in the future. However changing an enum member is a breaking change and can create significant problems. There is no need to reserve an enum member since a new member can be added in the future, and such an addition will usually not be a breaking change.

rules.title: Method signatures should not contain nested generic types
rules.desc: A nested type is a type argument that is also a generic type. Calling a method with such a nested type argument requires complicated and confusing code. It should be avoided as much as possible.

rules.title: All type parameters should be used in the parameter list to enable type inference
rules.desc: Type inference enables the call of a generic method without explicitly specifying its type arguments. This is not possible when a parameter type is missing from the argument list.

rules.title: Base class methods should not be hidden
rules.desc: When a method in a derived class has:

rules.title: Enumerations should have "Int32" storage
rules.desc: By default the storage type of an enum is Int32. In most cases it is not necessary to change this. In particular you will not achieve any performance gain by using a smaller data type (e.g. Byte) and may limit future uses.

rules.title: Interfaces should not be empty
rules.desc: Empty interfaces should be avoided as they do not provide any functional requirements for implementing classes.

rules.title: Child class fields should not differ from parent class fields only by capitalization
rules.desc: Having a field in a child class with a name that differs from a parent class' field only by capitalization is sure to cause confusion. Such child class fields should be renamed.

rules.title: Assemblies should be marked with "NeutralResourcesLanguageAttribute"
rules.desc: It is important to inform the ResourceManager of the language used to display the resources of the neutral culture for an assembly. This improves lookup performance for the first resource loaded.

rules.title: Exceptions should provide standard constructors
rules.desc: Exceptions types should provide the following constructors:

rules.title: Classes implementing "IEquatable<T>" should be sealed
rules.desc: When a class implements the IEquatable<T> interface, it enters a contract that, in effect, states "I know how to compare two instances of type T or any type derived from T for equality.". However if that class is derived, it is very unlikely that the base class will know how to make a meaningful comparison. Therefore that implicit contract is now broken.

rules.title: OS commands should not rely on PATH resolution
rules.desc: Executing an OS command without specifying an absolute or relative path exposes the application to PATH-hijacking attacks.

rules.title: Interface methods should be callable by derived types
rules.desc: When a base type explicitly implements a public interface method, property or event, that member is only accessible in derived types through a reference to the current instance (namely this). If the derived type explicitly overrides that interface member, the base implementation becomes inaccessible.

rules.title: Strings should be normalized to uppercase
rules.desc: Certain characters, once normalized to lowercase, cannot make a round trip. That is, they can not be converted from one locale to another and then accurately restored to their original characters.

rules.title: Type names should not match namespaces
rules.desc: When a type name matches the name of a publicly defined namespace, for instance one in the .NET framework class library, it leads to confusion and makes the library that much harder to use.

rules.title: Generics should be used when appropriate
rules.desc: When a reference parameter (keyword ref) is used, the passed argument type must exactly match the reference parameter type. This means that to be able to pass a derived type, it must be cast and assigned to a variable of the proper type. Use of generic methods eliminates that cumbersome down casting and should therefore be preferred.

rules.title: Properties should be preferred
rules.desc: Properties are accessed like fields which makes them easier to use.

rules.title: Operators should be overloaded consistently
rules.desc: When overloading some arithmetic operator overloads, it is very important to make sure that all related operators and methods are consistent in their implementation.

rules.title: Types should not extend outdated base types
rules.desc: With the advent of .NET Framework 2.0, certain practices and types have become obsolete.

rules.title: Literals should not be passed as localized parameters
rules.desc: String literals embedded in the source code will not be localized properly.

rules.title: Overloads with a "CultureInfo" or an "IFormatProvider" parameter should be used
rules.desc: When a System.Globalization.CultureInfo or IFormatProvider object is not supplied, the default value that is supplied by the overloaded member might not have the effect that you want in all locales.

rules.title: Locales should be set for data types
rules.desc: When you create a DataTable or DataSet, you should set the locale explicitly. By default, the locale for these types is the current culture. For data that is stored in a database or file and is shared globally, the locale should ordinarily be set to the invariant culture (CultureInfo.InvariantCulture).

rules.title: Overloads with a "StringComparison" parameter should be used
rules.desc: Many string operations, the Compare and Equals methods in particular, provide an overload that accepts a StringComparison enumeration value as a parameter. Calling these overloads and explicitly providing this parameter makes your code clearer and easier to maintain.

rules.title: Property names should not match get methods
rules.desc: Properties and Get method should have names that makes them clearly distinguishable.

rules.title: Non-abstract attributes should be sealed
rules.desc: The .NET framework class library provides methods for retrieving custom attributes. Sealing the attribute eliminates the search through the inheritance hierarchy, and can improve performance.

rules.title: "params" should be used instead of "varargs"
rules.desc: A method using the VarArgs calling convention is not Common Language Specification (CLS) compliant and might not be accessible across programming languages, while the params keyword works the same way and is CLS compliant.

rules.title: Operator overloads should have named alternatives
rules.desc: Operator overloading is convenient but unfortunately not portable across languages. To be able to access the same functionality from another language you need to provide an alternate named method following the convention:

rules.title: Non-flags enums should not be marked with "FlagsAttribute"
rules.desc: This rule raises an issue when an externally visible enumeration is marked with FlagsAttribute and one, or more, of its values is not a power of 2 or a combination of the other defined values.

rules.title: Method overloads should be grouped together
rules.desc: For clarity, all overloads of the same method should be grouped together. That lets both users and maintainers quickly understand all the current available options.

rules.title: Duplicate values should not be passed as arguments
rules.desc: There are valid cases for passing a variable multiple times into the same method call, but usually doing so is a mistake, and something else was intended for one of the arguments.

rules.title: Collection elements should not be replaced unconditionally
rules.desc: Storing a value inside a collection at a given key or index and then unconditionally overwriting it without reading the initial value is a case of a "dead store".

rules.title: Methods should not have identical implementations
rules.desc: Two methods having the same implementation are suspicious. It might be that something else was intended. Or the duplication is intentional, which becomes a maintenance burden.

rules.title: Empty collections should not be accessed or iterated
rules.desc: When a collection is empty, iterating it has no effect. Doing so anyway is likely a bug; either population was accidentally omitted, or the iteration needs to be revised.

rules.title: Classes should implement their "ExportAttribute" interfaces
rules.desc: The Attributed Programming Model, also known as Attribute-oriented programming (@OP), is a programming model used to embed attributes within codes.

rules.title: Native methods should be wrapped
rules.desc: Native methods are functions that reside in libraries outside the .NET runtime. Calling them is helpful for interoperability with applications and libraries written in other programming languages, mainly when performing platform-specific operations. However, doing so comes with additional risks since it means stepping out of the memory-safety model of the runtime. It is therefore highly recommended to take extra steps, like input validation, when invoking native methods. Making the native method private and providing a wrapper that performs these additional steps is the best way to do so.

rules.title: Null checks should not be combined with "is" operator checks
rules.desc: There’s no need to null test in conjunction with an is test. null is not an instance of anything, so a null check is redundant.

rules.title: Windows Forms entry points should be marked with STAThread
rules.desc: When an assembly uses Windows Forms (classes and interfaces from the System.Windows.Forms namespace) its entry point should be marked with the STAThreadAttribute to indicate that the threading model should be "Single-Threaded Apartment" (STA) which is the only one supported by Windows Forms.

rules.title: Members should not have conflicting transparency annotations
rules.desc: Transparency attributes in the .NET Framework, designed to protect security-critical operations, can lead to ambiguities and vulnerabilities when declared at different levels such as both for the class and a method.

rules.title: Serialization constructors should be secured
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.
rules.obsolete: This rule has been deprecated since 9.14

rules.title: "P/Invoke" methods should not be visible
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:csharpsquid:S4200} instead.

rules.title: Events should have proper arguments
rules.desc: When raising an event, two arguments are expected by the EventHandler delegate: Sender and event-data. There are three guidelines regarding these parameters:

rules.title: Extension methods should not extend "object"
rules.desc: ﻿Creating an extension method that extends object is not recommended because it makes the method available on every type. Extensions should be applied at the most specialized level possible, and that is very unlikely to be object.

rules.title: Extensions should be in separate namespaces
rules.desc: It makes little sense to create an extension method when it is possible to just add that method to the class itself.

rules.title: "ConstructorArgument" parameters should exist in constructors
rules.desc: When creating a custom Markup Extension that accepts parameters in WPF, the ConstructorArgument markup must be used to identify the discrete properties that match these parameters. However since this is done via a string, the compiler won’t give you any warning in case there are typos.

rules.title: Methods should be named according to their synchronicities
rules.desc: According to the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP), methods returning either a System.Threading.Tasks.Task or a System.Threading.Tasks.Task<TResult> are considered "asynchronous". Such methods should use the Async suffix. Conversely methods which do not return such Tasks should not have an "Async" suffix in their names.

rules.title: Getters and setters should access the expected fields
rules.desc: Properties provide a way to enforce encapsulation by providing accessors that give controlled access to private fields. However, in classes with multiple fields, it is not unusual that copy-and-paste is used to quickly create the needed properties, which can result in the wrong field being accessed by a getter or setter.

rules.title: "Shared" parts should not be created with "new"
rules.desc: Marking a class with PartCreationPolicy(CreationPolicy.Shared), which is part of Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), means that a single, shared instance of the exported object will be created. Therefore it doesn’t make sense to create new instances using the constructor and it will most likely result in unexpected behaviours.

rules.title: Secure random number generators should not output predictable values
rules.desc: Cryptographic operations often rely on unpredictable random numbers to enhance security. These random numbers are created by cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators (CSPRNG). It is important not to use a predictable seed with these random number generators otherwise the random numbers will also become predictable.

rules.title: Weak SSL/TLS protocols should not be used
rules.desc: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

rules.title: Cryptographic keys should be robust
rules.desc: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

rules.title: "PartCreationPolicyAttribute" should be used with "ExportAttribute"
rules.desc: To customize the default behavior for an export in the Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), applying the PartCreationPolicyAttribute is necessary. For the PartCreationPolicyAttribute to be meaningful in the context of an export, the class must also be annotated with the ExportAttribute.

rules.title: AES encryption algorithm should be used with secured mode
rules.desc: Encryption algorithms can be used with various modes. Some combinations are not secured:

rules.title: LDAP connections should be authenticated
rules.desc: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) servers provide two main authentication methods: the SASL and Simple ones. The Simple Authentication method also breaks down into three different mechanisms:

rules.title: Parameter validation in yielding methods should be wrapped
rules.desc: Because of the way yield methods are rewritten by the compiler (they become lazily evaluated state machines) any exceptions thrown during the parameters check will happen only when the collection is iterated over. That could happen far away from the source of the buggy code.

rules.title: Parameter validation in "async"/"await" methods should be wrapped
rules.desc: Because of the way async/await methods are rewritten by the compiler, any exceptions thrown during the parameters check are captured in the returned Task and will only be observed when the task is awaited. That could happen far away from the source of the buggy code or never happen for fire-and-forget tasks.

rules.title: Calls to "async" methods should not be blocking
rules.desc: Making blocking calls to async methods transforms code that was intended to be asynchronous into a blocking operation. Doing so can cause deadlocks and unexpected blocking of context threads.

rules.title: Unread "private" fields should be removed
rules.desc: Private fields which are written but never read are a case of "dead store". Changing the value of such a field is useless and most probably indicates an error in the code.

rules.title: CSRF protections should not be disabled
rules.desc: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) forces an authenticated user to perform unintended state-changing actions in a web application. This rule detects when CSRF protection is explicitly disabled or missing from an application.

rules.title: Debugging features should not be enabled in production
rules.desc: Development tools and frameworks usually have options to make debugging easier for developers, but these features should never be enabled for applications deployed in production.

rules.title: "default" clauses should be first or last
rules.desc: The switch statement is a conditional statement that executes a sequence of instructions based on patterns matching the provided value.

rules.title: Exposing HTTP endpoints is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Exposing HTTP endpoints is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: "DebuggerDisplayAttribute" strings should reference existing members
rules.desc: The DebuggerDisplayAttribute is used to determine how an object is displayed in the debugger window.

rules.title: ASP.NET HTTP request validation feature should not be disabled
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:csharpsquid:S5753} instead.

rules.title: "new Guid()" should not be used
rules.desc: When the syntax new Guid() (i.e. parameterless instantiation) is used, it must be that one of three things is wanted:

rules.title: Calls to delegate's method "BeginInvoke" should be paired with calls to "EndInvoke"
rules.desc: When calling the BeginInvoke method of a delegate, resources are allocated that are only freed up when EndInvoke is called. Failing to pair BeginInvoke with EndInvoke can lead to resource leaks and incomplete asynchronous calls.

rules.title: Non-async "Task/Task<T>" methods should not return null
rules.desc: Returning null from a non-async Task/Task<TResult> method will cause a NullReferenceException at runtime if the method is awaited. This problem can be avoided by returning Task.CompletedTask or Task.FromResult<TResult>(null) respectively.

rules.title: Start index should be used instead of calling Substring
rules.desc: It is important to be careful when searching for characters within a substring. Let’s consider the following example:

rules.title: Comments should not be empty
rules.desc: Empty comments, as shown in the example, hurt readability and might indicate an oversight.

rules.title: Executing OS commands is security-sensitive
rules.desc: OS commands are security-sensitive. For example, their use has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Using regular expressions is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:roslyn.sonaranalyzer.security.cs:S2631} instead.

rules.title: Encrypting data is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:csharpsquid:S4426}, {rule:csharpsquid:S5542}, {rule:csharpsquid:S5547} instead.

rules.title: Weak hashing algorithms should not be used
rules.desc: Using a weak hashing algorithm to protect sensitive data can compromise the security guarantees the hash is meant to provide.

rules.title: Configuring loggers is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Handling files is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Handling files is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Executing XPath expressions is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Executing XPATH expressions is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Using Sockets is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Using command line arguments is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Sending HTTP requests is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Sending HTTP requests is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Reading the Standard Input is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Server certificates should be verified during SSL/TLS connections
rules.desc: This vulnerability makes it possible that an encrypted communication is intercepted.

rules.title: Controlling permissions is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: "ValueTask" should be consumed correctly
rules.desc: ValueTask<TResult> provides a value type that wraps a Task<TResult> and the corresponding TResult. It was introduced in .NET Core 2.0 to optimize memory allocation when functions return their results synchronously.

rules.title: Expanding archive files should not be done without controlling resource consumption
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy should be restricted to trusted origins
rules.desc: Setting an overly permissive Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy allows malicious websites to read responses from your application on behalf of authenticated users.

rules.title: Clear-text protocols should not be used
rules.desc: Using clear-text protocols exposes data in transit to eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: Passwords should not be stored in plaintext or with a fast hashing algorithm
rules.desc: The improper storage of passwords poses a significant security risk to software applications. This vulnerability arises when passwords are stored in plaintext or with a fast hashing algorithm. To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker typically requires access to the stored passwords.

rules.title: Temporary files should not be created in publicly writable directories
rules.desc: Using publicly writable directories such as /tmp to store temporary files exposes an application to race condition vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Insecure temporary file creation methods should not be used
rules.desc: Temporary files are considered insecurely created when the file existence check is performed separately from the actual file creation. Such a situation can occur when creating temporary files using normal file handling functions or when using dedicated temporary file handling functions that are not atomic.

rules.title: Encryption algorithms should be used with secure mode and padding scheme
rules.desc: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

rules.title: Cipher algorithms should be robust
rules.desc: This vulnerability makes it possible that the cleartext of the encrypted message might be recoverable without prior knowledge of the key.

rules.title: JWT should be signed and verified with strong cipher algorithms
rules.desc: This vulnerability allows forging of JSON Web Tokens to impersonate other users.

rules.title: HTTP request content length should be limited
rules.desc: Enforcing a maximum HTTP request content length limits how much data the server must accept per request, which helps control resource use and reduces the risk of denial-of-service attacks.

rules.title: ASP.NET Request Validation should not be disabled
rules.desc: ASP.NET 1.1+ comes with a Request Validation feature that rejects requests containing un-encoded HTML, acting as a first layer of protection against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

rules.title: Serializable objects should validate data during deserialization
rules.desc: Serializable objects that lack data validation during deserialization can be exploited by attackers to bypass security checks.

rules.title: Types allowed to be deserialized should be restricted
rules.desc: Deserialization is the process of converting serialized data (such as objects or data structures) back into their original form. Types allowed to be unserialized should be strictly controlled.

rules.title: Regular expressions should be syntactically valid
rules.desc: Regular expressions have their own syntax that is understood by regular expression engines. Those engines will throw an exception at runtime if they are given a regular expression that does not conform to that syntax.

rules.title: Use a testable date/time provider
rules.desc: One of the principles of a unit test is that it must have full control of the system under test. This is problematic when production code includes calls to static methods, which cannot be changed or controlled. Date/time functions are usually provided by system libraries as static methods.

rules.title: XML signatures should be validated securely
rules.desc: XML signatures are a method used to ensure the integrity and authenticity of XML documents. However, if XML signatures are not validated securely, it can lead to potential vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Secrets should not be hard-coded
rules.desc: Hard-coding secrets in source code or binaries makes it easy for attackers to extract sensitive information, especially in distributed or open-source applications. This practice exposes credentials and tokens, increasing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches.

rules.title: Azure Functions should be stateless
rules.desc: An Azure Function should be stateless as there’s no control over where and when function instances are provisioned and de-provisioned. Managing and storing data/state between requests can lead to inconsistencies. If, for any reason, you need to have a stateful function, consider using the Durable Functions extension of Azure Functions.

rules.title: Client instances should not be recreated on each Azure Function invocation
rules.desc: To avoid holding more connections than necessary and to avoid potentially exhausting the number of available sockets when using HttpClient, DocumentClient, QueueClient, ConnectionMultiplexer or Azure Storage clients, consider:

rules.title: Azure Functions should use Structured Error Handling
rules.desc: The top-most level of an Azure Function code should include a try/catch block to capture and log all errors so you can monitor the health of the application effectively. In case a retry policy has been defined for your Azure Function, you should rethrow any errors that should result in a retry.

rules.title: Calls to "async" methods should not be blocking in Azure Functions
rules.desc: Making blocking calls to async methods transforms the code into a synchronous operation. Doing so inside an Azure Function can lead to thread pool exhaustion.

rules.title: Azure Functions should log all failures
rules.desc: Capturing and logging errors is critical to monitoring the health of your Azure Functions application.

rules.title: Interfaces for durable entities should satisfy the restrictions
rules.desc: The recommended way to access Azure Durable Entities is through generated proxy objects with the help of interfaces.

rules.title: Regular expressions should be executed with a timeout
rules.desc: Regular expressions without a timeout can be exploited to cause a Denial-of-Service attack.

rules.title: Blocks should not be synchronized on local variables
rules.desc: Locking on a local variable can undermine synchronization because two different threads running the same method in parallel will potentially lock on different instances of the same object, allowing them to access the synchronized block at the same time.

rules.title: "ExcludeFromCodeCoverage" attributes should include a justification
rules.desc: The ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is used to exclude portions of code from code coverage reporting. It is a bad practice to retain code that is not covered by unit tests. In .Net 5, the Justification property was added to the ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute as an opportunity to document the rationale for the exclusion. This rule raises an issue when no such justification is given.

rules.title: Avoid using "DateTime.Now" for benchmarking or timing operations
rules.desc: The rule targets the use of DateTime.Now call followed by some arithmetic operation.

rules.title: Always set the "DateTimeKind" when creating new "DateTime" instances
rules.desc: Not knowing the Kind of the DateTime object that an application is using can lead to misunderstandings when displaying or comparing them. Explicitly setting the Kind property helps the application to stay consistent, and its maintainers understand what kind of date is being managed. To achieve this, when instantiating a new DateTime object you should always use a constructor overload that allows you to define the Kind property.

rules.title: Use UTC when recording DateTime instants
rules.desc: You should avoid recording time instants with the use of property DateTime.Now. The property DateTime.Now returns the current date and time expressed in the machine’s local time without containing any timezone-related information (for example, the offset from Coordinated Universal Time). Not having this information means that if you need to display this DateTime object or use it for computations in another machine placed in a different time zone, you won’t be able to reconstruct it in the second machine’s local time without knowing the origin’s offset. This will likely lead to confusion and potential bugs.

rules.title: Use "DateTimeOffset" instead of "DateTime"
rules.desc: This rule recommends using DateTimeOffset instead of DateTime for projects targeting .NET Framework 2.0 or later.

rules.title: Use "TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById" without converting the timezones with "TimezoneConverter"
rules.desc: Since .NET 6 you don’t have to use the TimeZoneConverter library to manually do the conversion between IANA and Windows timezones. The .NET 6.0 introduced new Time Zone enhancements, one being the TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById(string timezone) method now accepts as input both IANA and Windows time zone IDs on any operating system with installed time zone data. TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById will automatically convert its input from IANA to Windows and vice versa if the requested time zone is not found on the system.

rules.title: Use a format provider when parsing date and time
rules.desc: When converting a string representation of a date and time to a DateTime object or any other temporal type with one of the available system parsing methods, you should always provide an IFormatProvider parameter.

rules.title: Don't hardcode the format when turning dates and times to strings
rules.desc: Hardcoding the date and time format strings can lead to formats that consumers misunderstand. Also, if the same format is meant to be used in multiple places, it is easier to make a mistake when it’s hardcoded instead of using a format provided by an IFormatProvider or using one of the standard format strings.

rules.title: Use the "UnixEpoch" field instead of creating "DateTime" instances that point to the beginning of the Unix epoch
rules.desc: With .NET Core the UnixEpoch field was introduced to DateTime and DateTimeOffset types. Using this field clearly states that the intention is to use the beginning of the Unix epoch.

rules.title: "Find" method should be used instead of the "FirstOrDefault" extension
rules.desc: Both the List.Find method and the Enumerable.FirstOrDefault method can be used to locate the first element that meets a specified condition within a collection. However, for List objects, List.Find may offer superior performance compared to Enumerable.FirstOrDefault. While the performance difference might be negligible for small collections, it can become significant for larger collections. This observation also holds true for ImmutableList and arrays.

rules.title: The collection-specific "TrueForAll" method should be used instead of the "All" extension
rules.desc: Both the List.TrueForAll method and the IEnumerable.All method can be used to check if all list elements satisfy a given condition in a collection. However, List.TrueForAll can be faster than IEnumerable.All for List objects. The performance difference may be minor for small collections, but for large collections, it can be noticeable.

rules.title: Collection-specific "Exists" method should be used instead of the "Any" extension
rules.desc: Both the List.Exists method and IEnumerable.Any method can be used to find the first element that satisfies a predicate in a collection. However, List.Exists can be faster than IEnumerable.Any for List objects, as well as requires significantly less memory. For small collections, the performance difference may be negligible, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies to ImmutableList and arrays too.

rules.title: The collection should be filtered before sorting by using "Where" before "OrderBy"
rules.desc: When working with LINQ in C#, it is recommended to pay attention to the order in which methods are chained, especially when using Where and OrderBy methods. It is advised to call the Where method before OrderBy because Where filters the elements of the sequence based on a given condition and returns a new sequence containing only the elements that satisfy that condition. Calling OrderBy before Where, may end up sorting elements that will be later discarded, which can lead to inefficiency. Conversely, calling Where before OrderBy, will first filter the sequence to include only the elements of interest, and then sort them based on the specified order.

rules.title: Prefer indexing instead of "Enumerable" methods on types implementing "IList"
rules.desc: Indexes in C# provide direct access to an element at a specific position within an array or collection. When compared to Enumerable methods, indexing can be more efficient for certain scenarios, such as iterating over a large collection, due to avoiding the overhead of checking the underlying collection type before accessing it.

rules.title: "Min/Max" properties of "Set" types should be used instead of the "Enumerable" extension methods
rules.desc: Both the Enumerable.Max extension method and the SortedSet<T>.Max property can be used to find the maximum value in a SortedSet<T>. However, SortedSet<T>.Max is much faster than Enumerable.Max. For small collections, the performance difference may be minor, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies for the Min property as well.

rules.title: "StartsWith" and "EndsWith" overloads that take a "char" should be used instead of the ones that take a "string"
rules.desc: With string.StartsWith(char) and string.EndsWith(char), only the first character of the string is compared to the provided character, whereas the string versions of those methods have to do checks about the current StringComparison and CultureInfo. Thus, the char overloads are significantly faster for default comparison scenarios.

rules.title: The lambda parameter should be used instead of capturing arguments in "ConcurrentDictionary" methods
rules.desc: When using the ConcurrentDictionary, there are many overloads of the GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate methods that take both a TKey argument and a lambda that expects a TKey parameter. This means that the right side of the lambda can be written using either the lambda’s parameter or the method’s argument. However, using the method’s argument leads to the lambda capturing it, and the compiler will need to generate a class and instantiate it before the call. This means memory allocations, as well as more time spend during Garbage Collection.

rules.title: "First" and "Last" properties of "LinkedList" should be used instead of the "First()" and "Last()" extension methods
rules.desc: Both the Enumerable.First extension method and the LinkedList<T>.First property can be used to find the first value in a LinkedList<T>. However, LinkedList<T>.First is much faster than Enumerable.First. For small collections, the performance difference may be minor, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies for the Last property as well.

rules.title: "Contains" should be used instead of "Any" for simple equality checks
rules.desc: When testing if a collection contains a specific item by simple equality, both ICollection.Contains(T item) and IEnumerable.Any(x ⇒ x == item) can be used. However, Any searches the data structure in a linear manner using a foreach loop, whereas Contains is considerably faster in some collection types, because of the underlying implementation. More specifically:

rules.title: "string.Create" should be used instead of "FormattableString"
rules.desc: In order to produce a formatted string, both string.Create and either FormattableString.Invariant or FormattableString.CurrentCulture can be used. However, string.Create rents array buffers from ArrayPool<char> making it more performant, as well as preventing unnecessary allocations and future stress on the Garbage Collector.

rules.title: Unsafe code blocks should not be used
rules.desc: Using unsafe code blocks bypasses the .NET runtime’s safety guarantees and can introduce memory corruption vulnerabilities that are invisible to the managed runtime.

rules.title: The code block contains too many logging calls
rules.desc: A code block should not contain too many logging statements of a specific level.

rules.title: Logging in a catch clause should pass the caught exception as a parameter.
rules.desc: This rule raises an issue on logging calls inside a catch clause that does not pass the raised Exception.

rules.title: Logging arguments should be passed to the correct parameter
rules.desc: Most logging frameworks have methods that take a log level, an event ID or an exception as a separate input next to the log format and its arguments. There is a high chance that if the log level, the event ID or the exception are passed as the arguments to the message format, it was a mistake. This rule is going to raise in that scenario.

rules.title: Logger field or property name should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Sharing some naming conventions is a key point to make it possible for a team to efficiently collaborate. This rule checks that the logger field or property name matches a provided regular expression.

rules.title: "Trace.Write" and "Trace.WriteLine" should not be used
rules.desc: Trace.Write and Trace.WriteLine methods are writing to the underlying output stream directly, bypassing the trace formatting and filtering performed by TraceListener.TraceEvent implementations. It is preferred to use Trace.TraceError, Trace.TraceWarning, and Trace.TraceInformation methods instead because they call the TraceEvent method which filters the trace output according to the TraceEventType (Error, Warning or Information) and enhance the output with additional information.

rules.title: Generic logger injection should match enclosing type
rules.desc: In most logging frameworks, it’s good practice to set the logger name to match its enclosing type, as enforced by {rule:csharpsquid:S3416}.

rules.title: Log message template placeholders should be in the right order
rules.desc: The positions of arguments in a logging call should match the positions of their message template placeholders.

rules.title: Log message template should be syntactically correct
rules.desc: A message template must conform to the specification. The rule raises an issue if the template string violates the template string grammar.

rules.title: "Trace.WriteLineIf" should not be used with "TraceSwitch" levels
rules.desc: The Trace.WriteLineIf Method from the System.Diagnostic.Trace facility writes a trace if the condition passed as the first parameter is true.

rules.title: Message template placeholders should be unique
rules.desc: Named placeholders in message templates should be unique. The meaning of the named placeholders is to store the value of the provided argument under that name, enabling easier log querying. Since the named placeholder is used multiple times, it cannot store the different values uniquely with each name hence not serving its original purpose. There can be different behaviours when using the same named placeholder multiple times:

rules.title: Use PascalCase for named placeholders
rules.desc: Within a message template each named placeholder should be in PascalCase.

rules.title: JWT secret keys should not be disclosed
rules.desc: Secret leaks often occur when a sensitive piece of authentication data is stored with the source code of an application. Considering the source code is intended to be deployed across multiple assets, including source code repositories or application hosting servers, the secrets might get exposed to an unintended audience.

rules.title: Blazor query parameter type should be supported
rules.desc: The SupplyParameterFromQuery attribute can be used to specify that a component parameter, of a routable component, comes from the query string.

rules.title: [JSInvokable] attribute should only be used on public methods
rules.desc: In Blazor, the [JSInvokable] attribute is used to annotate a method, enabling it to be invoked from JavaScript code. The prerequisite for this functionality is that the method must be declared as public. Otherwise, a runtime error will be triggered when an attempt is made to call the method from JavaScript.

rules.title: Component parameter type should match the route parameter type constraint
rules.desc: In Blazor, when a route parameter constraint is applied, the value is automatically cast to the corresponding component parameter type. If the constraint type does not match the component parameter type, it can lead to confusion and potential runtime errors due to unsuccessful casting. Therefore, it is crucial to ensure that the types of route parameters and component parameters match to prevent such issues and maintain code clarity.

rules.title: Using lambda expressions in loops should be avoided in Blazor markup section
rules.desc: In Blazor, using lambda expressions as event handlers when the UI elements are rendered in a loop can lead to negative user experiences and performance issues. This is particularly noticeable when rendering a large number of elements.

rules.title: Parameters with SupplyParameterFromQuery attribute should be used only in routable components
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Backslash should be avoided in route templates
rules.desc: Backslash characters (\) should be avoided in route templates.

rules.title: ASP.NET controller actions should not have a route template starting with "/"
rules.desc: Route templates for ASP.NET controller actions, defined via a RouteAttribute or any derivation of HttpMethodAttribute, should not start with "/".

rules.title: Use model binding instead of reading raw request data
rules.desc: The HttpRequest class provides access to the raw request data through the QueryString, Headers, and Forms properties. However, whenever possible it is recommended to use model binding instead of directly accessing the input data.

rules.title: A Route attribute should be added to the controller when a route template is specified at the action level
rules.desc: When a route template is defined through an attribute on an action method, conventional routing for that action is disabled. To maintain good practice, it’s recommended not to combine conventional and attribute-based routing within a single controller to avoid unpredicted behavior. As such, the controller should exclude itself from conventional routing by applying a [Route] attribute.

rules.title: Controllers should not have mixed responsibilities
rules.desc: ASP.NET controllers should not have mixed responsibilities. Following the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), they should be kept lean and focused on a single, separate concern. In short, they should have a single reason to change.

rules.title: API Controllers should derive from ControllerBase instead of Controller
rules.desc: In ASP.NET Core, controllers usually inherit either from ControllerBase or Controller. If a controller does not use any View-specific functionality, it is recommended to inherit from ControllerBase.

rules.title: You should pool HTTP connections with HttpClientFactory
rules.desc: In frequently used code paths, such as controller actions, you should avoid using the HttpClient directly and opt for one of the IHttpClientFactory-based mechanisms instead. This way, you avoid wasting resources and creating performance overhead.

rules.title: Value type property used as input in a controller action should be nullable, required or annotated with the JsonRequiredAttribute to avoid under-posting.
rules.desc: "Under-posting" refers to a situation where a client sends less data than expected to the server during an HTTP request, for example when the client omits some properties from the request body that the server expects to receive.

rules.title: REST API actions should be annotated with an HTTP verb attribute
rules.desc: When building a REST API, it’s recommended to annotate the controller actions with the available HTTP attributes to be precise about what your API supports.

rules.title: Awaitable method should be used
rules.desc: In an async method, any blocking operations should be avoided.

rules.title: ModelState.IsValid should be called in controller actions
rules.desc: In the context of ASP.NET Core MVC web applications, both model binding and model validation are processes that take place prior to the execution of a controller action. It is imperative for the application to examine the ModelState.IsValid and respond accordingly.

rules.title: Actions that return a value should be annotated with ProducesResponseTypeAttribute containing the return type
rules.desc: In an ASP.NET Core Web API, controller actions can optionally return a result value. If a controller action returns a value in the happy path, for example ControllerBase.Ok(Object), annotating the action with one of the [ProducesResponseType] overloads that describe the type is recommended.

rules.title: Content Security Policies should be restrictive
rules.desc: The Content Security Policy (CSP) is a computer security standard that serves as an additional layer of protection against various types of attacks, including Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and clickjacking. It provides a set of standard procedures for loading resources by user agents, which can help to mitigate the risk of content injection vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Identifiers should not conflict with the C# 14 "field" contextual keyword
rules.desc: This rule raises an issue when code uses 'field' as an identifier in contexts where it conflicts with the new field contextual keyword introduced in C# 14.

rules.title: Identifiers should not conflict with the C# 14 "extension" contextual keyword
rules.desc: Identifiers named extension should be renamed or use the @ escape prefix to avoid breaking changes in C# 14 or later.

rules.title: Return types named "partial" should be escaped with "@"
rules.desc: Using partial as a return type identifier will cause a compilation error when upgrading to C# 14.

rules.title: "scoped" should be escaped when used as an identifier or type name in parenthesized lambda parameter lists
rules.desc: Using scoped as a type name in lambda parameter lists will cause a compilation error when upgrading to C# 14 or later.

rules.title: The overload accepting a 'CancellationToken' should be used
rules.desc: When a CancellationToken is available but not forwarded to a method that has an overload accepting one, the cancellation request is silently ignored.

rules.title: Null-forgiving operators should not be redundant
rules.desc: The null-forgiving operator ! tells the compiler "trust me, this expression is not null", suppressing any nullable warning that would otherwise be raised at this position.

rules.title: Null-forgiving operators should not be used when nullable warnings are disabled
rules.desc: The null-forgiving operator (!) should only be used to suppress a nullable warning that the compiler would otherwise report. When nullable warnings are disabled at that point in the code, there is no warning to suppress, and the operator is redundant.
