Class names should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently.

rules.title: Lines should not be too long
rules.desc: Scrolling horizontally to see a full line of code lowers the code readability.

rules.title: Files should not have too many lines of code
rules.desc: When a source file grows too much, it can accumulate numerous responsibilities and become challenging to understand and maintain.

rules.title: Tabulation characters should not be used
rules.desc: The tab width can differ from one development environment to another. Using tabs may require other developers to configure their environment (text editor, preferences, etc.) to read source code.

rules.title: Procedures should not have too many parameters
rules.desc: Procedures with a long parameter list are difficult to use because maintainers must figure out the role of each parameter and keep track of their position.

rules.title: Nested blocks of code should not be left empty
rules.desc: An empty code block is confusing. It will require some effort from maintainers to determine if it is intentional or indicates the implementation is incomplete.

rules.title: General or reserved exceptions should never be thrown
rules.desc: This rule raises an issue when a generic exception (such as Exception, SystemException, ApplicationException, IndexOutOfRangeException, NullReferenceException, OutOfMemoryException or ExecutionEngineException) is thrown.

rules.title: Interface names should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Sharing some naming conventions is a key point to make it possible for a team to efficiently collaborate.

rules.title: Local variable names should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Local variables should be named consistently to communicate intent and improve maintainability. Rename your local variable to follow your project’s naming convention to address this issue.

rules.title: Generic type parameter names should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Inconsistent naming conventions can lead to confusion and errors when working in a team. This rule ensures that all generic type parameter names follow a consistent naming convention by checking them against a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Statements should be on separate lines
rules.desc: Putting multiple statements on a single line lowers the code readability and makes debugging the code more complex.

rules.title: "If ... ElseIf" constructs should end with "Else" clauses
rules.desc: This rule applies whenever an If statement is followed by one or more ElseIf statements; the final ElseIf should be followed by an Else statement.

rules.title: "Select" statements should end with a "Case Else" clause
rules.desc: The requirement for a final Case Else clause is defensive programming.

rules.title: Control flow statements "If", "For", "For Each", "Do", "While", "Select" and "Try" should not be nested too deeply
rules.desc: Nested control flow statements If, Select, For, For Each, While, Do, and Try are often key ingredients in creating what’s known as "Spaghetti code". This code smell can make your program difficult to understand and maintain.

rules.title: Procedures should not have too many lines of code
rules.desc: A procedure that grows too large tends to aggregate too many responsibilities.

rules.title: Comments should not be located at the end of lines of code
rules.desc: This rule verifies that single-line comments are not located at the ends of lines of code. The main idea behind this rule is that in order to be really readable, trailing comments would have to be properly written and formatted (correct alignment, no interference with the visual structure of the code, not too long to be visible) but most often, automatic code formatters would not handle this correctly: the code would end up less readable. Comments are far better placed on the previous empty line of code, where they will always be visible and properly formatted.

rules.title: "GoTo" statements should not be used
rules.desc: GoTo is an unstructured control flow statement. It makes code less readable and maintainable. Structured control flow statements such as If, For, While, or Exit should be used instead.

rules.title: Parameter names should match base declaration
rules.desc: Parameters are part of the method signature and its identity.

rules.title: Finalize method should not throw exceptions
rules.desc: The Finalize methods are used to perform any necessary final clean-up when the garbage collector is collecting a class instance. The programmer has no control over when the Finalize method is called; the garbage collector decides when to call it.

rules.title: Mergeable "if" statements should be combined
rules.desc: Nested code - blocks of code inside blocks of code - is eventually necessary, but increases complexity. This is why keeping the code as flat as possible, by avoiding unnecessary nesting, is considered a good practice.

rules.title: Expressions should not be too complex
rules.desc: Complex boolean expressions are hard to read and so to maintain.

rules.title: URIs should not be hardcoded
rules.desc: Hard-coding a URI makes it difficult to test a program for a variety of reasons:

rules.title: Redundant pairs of parentheses should be removed
rules.desc: The use of parentheses, even those not required to enforce a desired order of operations, can clarify the intent behind a piece of code. However, redundant pairs of parentheses could be misleading and should be removed.

rules.title: "Obsolete" attributes should include explanations
rules.desc: The Obsolete attribute can be applied with or without a message argument. Marking something Obsolete without including advice on why it’s obsolete or what to use instead will lead maintainers to waste time trying to figure those things out.

rules.title: Boolean literals should not be redundant
rules.desc: A boolean literal can be represented in two different ways: True or False. They can be combined with logical operators (Not, And, Or, =) to produce logical expressions that represent truth values. However, comparing a boolean literal to a variable or expression that evaluates to a boolean value is unnecessary and can make the code harder to read and understand. The more complex a boolean expression is, the harder it will be for developers to understand its meaning and expected behavior, and it will favour the introduction of new bugs.

rules.title: Deprecated code should be removed
rules.desc: This rule is meant to be used as a way to track code which is marked as being deprecated. Deprecated code should eventually be removed.

rules.title: Track uses of "FIXME" tags
rules.desc: FIXME tags are commonly used to mark places where a bug is suspected, but which the developer wants to deal with later.

rules.title: Track uses of "TODO" tags
rules.desc: Developers often use TODO tags to mark areas in the code where additional work or improvements are needed but are not implemented immediately. However, these TODO tags sometimes get overlooked or forgotten, leading to incomplete or unfinished code. This rule aims to identify and address unattended TODO tags to ensure a clean and maintainable codebase. This description explores why this is a problem and how it can be fixed to improve the overall code quality.

rules.title: Useless "if(true) {...}" and "if(false){...}" blocks should be removed
rules.desc: if statements with conditions that are always false have the effect of making blocks of code non-functional. if statements with conditions that are always true are completely redundant, and make the code less readable.

rules.title: "End" statements should not be used
rules.desc: End statements exit the control flow of the program in an unstructured way. This statement stops code execution immediately without executing Dispose or Finalize methods, or executing Finally blocks. Therefore, it should be avoided.

rules.title: "Select...Case" clauses should not have too many lines of code
rules.desc: The Select...Case statement should be used only to clearly define some new branches in the control flow. As soon as a case clause contains too many statements this highly decreases the readability of the overall control flow statement. In such case, the content of the case clause should be extracted into a dedicated procedure.

rules.title: "Any()" should be used to test for emptiness
rules.desc: Using .Count() to test for emptiness works, but using .Any() makes the intent clearer, and the code more readable. However, there are some cases where special attention should be paid:

rules.title: Exceptions should not be thrown in finally blocks
rules.desc: If an exception is already being thrown within the try block or caught in a catch block, throwing another exception in the finally block will override the original exception. This means that the original exception’s message and stack trace will be lost, potentially making it challenging to diagnose and troubleshoot the root cause of the problem.

rules.title: Unused procedure parameters should be removed
rules.desc: A typical code smell known as unused function parameters refers to parameters declared in a function but not used anywhere within the function’s body. While this might seem harmless at first glance, it can lead to confusion and potential errors in your code. Disregarding the values passed to such parameters, the function’s behavior will be the same, but the programmer’s intention won’t be clearly expressed anymore. Therefore, removing function parameters that are not being utilized is considered best practice.

rules.title: Methods should not be empty
rules.desc: An empty method is generally considered bad practice and can lead to confusion, readability, and maintenance issues. Empty methods bring no functionality and are misleading to others as they might think the method implementation fulfills a specific and identified requirement.

rules.title: String literals should not be duplicated
rules.desc: Duplicated string literals make the process of refactoring complex and error-prone, as any change would need to be propagated on all occurrences.

rules.title: Array designators "()" should be on the type, not the variable
rules.desc: Array designators should always be located on the type for better code readability. Otherwise, developers must look both at the type and the variable name to know whether or not a variable is an array.

rules.title: Method parameters and caught exceptions should not be reassigned
rules.desc: While it is technically correct to assign to parameters from within method bodies, doing so before the parameter value is read is likely a bug. Instead, initial values of parameters should be, if not treated as readonly then at least read before reassignment.

rules.title: "Select" statements should have at least 3 "Case" clauses
rules.desc: switch statements are useful when there are many different cases depending on the value of the same expression.

rules.title: IP addresses should not be hardcoded
rules.desc: IP addresses hardcoded in source code couple the application to a specific infrastructure configuration. Today’s services have an ever-changing architecture due to their scaling and redundancy needs. When an IP address changes, every hardcoded occurrence must be found and updated, which has an impact on development, delivery, and deployment:

rules.title: Track lack of copyright and license headers
rules.desc: Each source file should start with a header stating file ownership and the license which must be used to distribute the application.

rules.title: "Select Case" statement with many "Case" clauses should have only one statement
rules.desc: When Select Case statements have large sets of multi-line Case clauses, the code becomes hard to read and maintain.

rules.title: Unused local variables should be removed
rules.desc: An unused local variable is a variable that has been declared but is not used anywhere in the block of code where it is defined. It is dead code, contributing to unnecessary complexity and leading to confusion when reading the code. Therefore, it should be removed from your code to maintain clarity and efficiency.

rules.title: Dynamically executing code is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Executing code dynamically is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Functions, procedures and properties should not be too complex
rules.desc: The cyclomatic complexity of a function, procedure or property should not exceed a defined threshold. Complex code can perform poorly and will in any case be difficult to understand and therefore to maintain.

rules.title: Functions and procedures should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all subroutine and function names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Strings should not be concatenated using "+" or "&" in a loop
rules.desc: StringBuilder is more efficient than string concatenation, especially when the operator is repeated over and over as in loops.

rules.title: The "&" operator should be used to concatenate strings
rules.desc: Consistently using the & operator for string concatenation make the developer intentions clear.

rules.title: Method parameters should follow a naming convention
rules.desc: Sharing some naming conventions is a key point to make it possible for a team to efficiently collaborate.

rules.title: Variables should not be self-assigned
rules.desc: There is no reason to re-assign a variable to itself. Either this statement is redundant and should be removed, or the re-assignment is a mistake and some other value or variable was intended for the assignment instead.

rules.title: Multiple variables should not be declared on the same line
rules.desc: Declaring multiple variable on one line is difficult to read.

rules.title: Loops with at most one iteration should be refactored
rules.desc: A loop statement with at most one iteration is equivalent to an If statement; the following block is executed only once.

rules.title: Identical expressions should not be used on both sides of a binary operator
rules.desc: Using the same value on either side of a binary operator is almost always a mistake. In the case of logical operators, it is either a copy/paste error and therefore a bug, or it is simply wasted code, and should be simplified. In the case of most binary mathematical operators, having the same value on both sides of an operator yields predictable results, and should be simplified.

rules.title: "Select Case" statements should not be nested
rules.desc: Nested Select Case structures are difficult to understand because you can easily confuse the cases of an inner Select Case as belonging to an outer statement. Therefore nested Select Case statements should be avoided.

rules.title: Related "If/ElseIf" statements should not have the same condition
rules.desc: A chain of If/ElseIf statements is evaluated from top to bottom. At most, only one branch will be executed: the first statement with a condition that evaluates to True. Therefore, duplicating a condition leads to unreachable code inside the duplicated condition block. Usually, this is due to a copy/paste error.

rules.title: Two branches in a conditional structure should not have exactly the same implementation
rules.desc: When the same code is duplicated in two or more separate branches of a conditional, it can make the code harder to understand, maintain, and can potentially introduce bugs if one instance of the code is changed but others are not.

rules.title: Boolean checks should not be inverted
rules.desc: It is needlessly complex to invert the result of a boolean comparison. The opposite comparison should be made instead.

rules.title: Invalid casts should be avoided
rules.desc: A cast is an explicit conversion, which is a way to tell the compiler the intent to convert from one type to another.

rules.title: Password hashing functions should use an unpredictable salt
rules.desc: This vulnerability increases the likelihood that attackers are able to compute the cleartext of password hashes.

rules.title: Credentials should not be hard-coded
rules.desc: Hard-coding credentials in source code or binaries makes it easy for attackers to extract sensitive information, especially in distributed or open-source applications. This practice exposes your application to significant security risks.

rules.title: SQL queries should not be dynamically formatted
rules.desc: Dynamically building SQL query strings can result in broken SQL syntax and open SQL injection attacks.

rules.title: Classes should not be empty
rules.desc: There is no good excuse for an empty class. If it’s being used simply as a common extension point, it should be replaced with an interface. If it was stubbed in as a placeholder for future development it should be fleshed-out. In any other case, it should be eliminated.

rules.title: Classes named like "Exception" should extend "Exception" or a subclass
rules.desc: Clear, communicative naming is important in code. It helps maintainers and API users understand the intentions for and uses of a unit of code. Using "exception" in the name of a class that does not extend Exception or one of its subclasses is a clear violation of the expectation that a class' name will indicate what it is and/or does.

rules.title: Short-circuit logic should be used in boolean contexts
rules.desc: Short-circuit evaluation is an evaluation strategy for Boolean operators, that doesn’t evaluate the second argument of the operator if it is not needed to determine the result of the operation.

rules.title: Locks should be released on all paths
rules.desc: To prevent potential deadlocks in an application, it is crucial to release any locks that are acquired within a method along all possible execution paths.

rules.title: "ToString()" method should not return Nothing
rules.desc: Calling ToString() on an object should always return a string. Thus, overriding the ToString method should never return Nothing because it breaks the method’s implicit contract, and as a result the consumer’s expectations.

rules.title: Arguments should be passed in the same order as the procedure parameters
rules.desc: Calling a procedure with argument variables whose names match the procedure parameter names but in a different order can cause confusion. It could indicate a mistake in the arguments' order, leading to unexpected results.

rules.title: Writing cookies is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Custom cryptographic algorithms should not be used
rules.desc: Cryptographic operations should use proven, standard algorithms rather than custom implementations.

rules.title: Null pointers should not be dereferenced
rules.desc: Accessing a Nothing value will always throw a NullReferenceException most likely causing an abrupt program termination.

rules.title: "NameOf" should be used
rules.desc: Because parameter names could be changed during refactoring, they should not be spelled out literally in strings. Instead, use NameOf(), and the string that’s output will always be correct.

rules.title: Namespace names should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all namespace names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Public constant members should not be used
rules.desc: Constant members are copied at compile time to the call sites, instead of being fetched at runtime.

rules.title: "Do" loops should not be used without a "While" or "Until" condition
rules.desc: A Do ... Loop without a While or Until condition must be terminated by an unstructured Exit Do statement. It is safer and more readable to use structured loops instead.

rules.title: Enumeration types should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all enum names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Enumeration values should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all enumeration value names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Enumeration type names should not have "Flags" or "Enum" suffixes
rules.desc: The information that an enumeration type is actually an enumeration or a set of flags should not be duplicated in its name.

rules.title: Flags enumerations should explicitly initialize all their members
rules.desc: When you annotate an Enum with the Flags attribute, you must not rely on the values that are automatically set by the language to the Enum members, but you should define the enumeration constants in powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). Automatic value initialization will set the first member to zero and increment the value by one for each subsequent member. As a result, you won’t be able to use the enum members with bitwise operators.

rules.title: Flags enumerations zero-value members should be named "None"
rules.desc: An enumeration can be decorated with the FlagsAttribute to indicate that it can be used as a bit field: a set of flags, that can be independently set and reset.

rules.title: Event handlers should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all even handler names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Events should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all even names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Event names should not have "Before" or "After" as a prefix or suffix
rules.desc: "After" and "Before" prefixes or suffixes should not be used to indicate pre and post events. The concepts of before and after should be given to events using the present and past tense.

rules.title: Indexed properties with more than one parameter should not be used
rules.desc: Indexed properties are meant to represent access to a logical collection. When multiple parameters are required, this design guideline may be violated, and refactoring the property into a method is preferable.

rules.title: Indexed properties should be named "Item"
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Line continuations should not be used
rules.desc: To improve the code readability, the explicit line continuation character, _, should not be used. Instead, it is better to break lines after an operator.

rules.title: Array literals should be used instead of array creation expressions
rules.desc: Array literals are more compact than array creation expressions.

rules.title: Fields should be private
rules.desc: Fields should not be part of an API, and therefore should always be private. Indeed, they cannot be added to an interface for instance, and validation cannot be added later on without breaking backward compatibility. Instead, developers should encapsulate their fields into properties. Explicit property getters and setters can be introduced for validation purposes or to smooth the transition to a newer system.

rules.title: "IsNot" should be used instead of "Not ... Is ..."
rules.desc: The ... IsNot ... syntax is more compact and more readable than the Not ... Is ... syntax.

rules.title: "On Error" statements should not be used
rules.desc: Prefer the use of Try ... Catch blocks instead of On Error statements.

rules.title: Optional parameters should not be used
rules.desc: The overloading mechanism should be used in place of optional parameters for several reasons:

rules.title: Private constants should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all Private Const field names comply with the provided regular expression.

rules.title: "Private Shared ReadOnly" fields should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all Private Shared ReadOnly field names comply with the provided regular expression.

rules.title: "Private" fields should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all Private field names match the provided regular expression.

rules.title: Properties should not make collection or array copies
rules.desc: Most developers expect property access to be as efficient as field access. However, if a property returns a copy of an array or collection, it will be much slower than a simple field access, contrary to the caller’s likely expectations. Therefore, such properties should be refactored into methods so that callers are not surprised by the unexpectedly poor performance.

rules.title: Properties should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that property names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Non-private constants should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private Const field names comply with the provided regular expression.

rules.title: Public methods should not have multidimensional array parameters
rules.desc: Using multidimensional and jagged arrays as method parameters in C# can be challenging for developers.

rules.title: Non-private fields should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private fields names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Non-private "Shared ReadOnly" fields should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private Shared ReadOnly fields names match a provided regular expression.

rules.title: Exceptions should not be thrown from property getters
rules.desc: Property getters should be simple operations that are always safe to call. If exceptions need to be thrown, it is best to convert the property to a method.

rules.title: Generic type parameter names should comply with a naming convention
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:vbnet:S119} instead.

rules.title: Signed types should be preferred to unsigned ones
rules.desc: Unsigned integers have different arithmetic operators than signed ones - operators that few developers understand. Therefore, signed types should be preferred where possible.

rules.title: "With" statements should be used for a series of calls to the same object
rules.desc: Using the With statement for a series of calls to the same object makes the code more readable.

rules.title: Write-only properties should not be used
rules.desc: Properties with only setters are confusing and counterintuitive. Instead, a property getter should be added if possible, or the property should be replaced with a setter method.

rules.title: Child class fields should not shadow parent class fields
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Arrays should be initialized using the "... = {}" syntax
rules.desc: The ... = {} syntax is more compact, more readable and less error-prone.

rules.title: Unnecessary bit operations should not be performed
rules.desc: Certain bitwise operations are not needed and should not be performed because their results are predictable.

rules.title: Shared resources should not be used for locking
rules.desc: The instance passed to the SyncLock statement should be a dedicated private field.

rules.title: Conditionally executed code should be reachable
rules.desc: Conditional expressions which are always true or false can lead to unreachable code.

rules.title: Boolean expressions should not be gratuitous
rules.desc: Gratuitous boolean expressions are conditions that do not change the evaluation of a program. This issue can indicate logical errors and affect the correctness of an application, as well as its maintainability.

rules.title: File permissions should not be set to world-accessible values
rules.desc: In Windows, "Everyone" group is similar and includes all members of the Authenticated Users group as well as the built-in Guest account, and several other built-in security accounts.

rules.title: "IndexOf" checks should not be for positive numbers
rules.desc: Most checks against an IndexOf value compare it with -1 because 0 is a valid index.

rules.title: "catch" clauses should do more than rethrow
rules.desc: A Catch clause that only rethrows the caught exception has the same effect as omitting the Catch altogether and letting it bubble up automatically.

rules.title: Non-existent operators like "=+" should not be used
rules.desc: Using operator pairs (=+ or =-) that look like reversed single operators (+= or -=) is confusing. They compile and run but do not produce the same result as their mirrored counterpart.

rules.title: 'Not' boolean operator should not be repeated
rules.desc: The repetition of the Not operator is usually a typo. The second operator invalidates the first one:

rules.title: "Thread.Sleep" should not be used in tests
rules.desc: Using Thread.Sleep in a test might introduce unpredictable and inconsistent results depending on the environment. Furthermore, it will block the thread, which means the system resources are not being fully used.

rules.title: "Exit Select" statements should not be used redundantly
rules.desc: Visual Basic .NET, unlike many other programming languages, has no "fall-through" for its Select cases. Each case already has an implicit Exit Select as its last instruction. It therefore is redundant to explicitly add one.

rules.title: Reflection should not be used to increase accessibility of classes, methods, or fields
rules.desc: Altering or bypassing the accessibility of classes, methods, or fields through reflection violates the encapsulation principle. This can break the internal contracts of the accessed target and lead to maintainability issues and runtime errors.

rules.title: "StringBuilder" data should be used
rules.desc: StringBuilder instances that never build a string clutter the code and worse are a drag on performance. Either they should be removed, or the missing ToString() call should be added.

rules.title: Cipher Block Chaining IVs should be unpredictable
rules.desc: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

rules.title: If operators should not be nested
rules.desc: Nested ternaries are hard to read and can make the order of operations complex to understand.

rules.title: Date and time should not be used as a type for primary keys
rules.desc: You should only set a property of a temporal type (like DateTime or DateTimeOffset) as the primary key of a table if the values are guaranteed to be unique.

rules.title: "Exit" statements should not be used
rules.desc: Exit Function, Exit Property, and Exit Sub are all poor, less-readable substitutes for a simple Return, and if used with code that should return a value (Exit Function and in some cases Exit Property) they could result in a NullReferenceException.

rules.title: "[ExpectedException]" should not be used
rules.desc: It should be clear to a casual reader what code a test is testing and what results are expected. Unfortunately, that’s not usually the case with the ExpectedException attribute since an exception could be thrown from almost any line in the method.

rules.title: Right operands of shift operators should be integers
rules.desc: Numbers can be shifted with the << and >> operators, but the right operand of the operation needs to be an int or a type that has an implicit conversion to int. However, when the left operand is an object, the compiler’s type checking is turned off, therfore you can pass anything to the right of a shift operator and have it compile. If the argument can’t be implicitly converted to int at runtime, a RuntimeBinderException will be raised.

rules.title: Classes should not have only "private" constructors
rules.desc: When a class has only a private constructor, it can’t be instantiated except within the class itself. Such classes can be considered dead code and should be fixed

rules.title: Type inheritance should not be recursive
rules.desc: Recursion is a technique used to define a problem in terms of the problem itself, usually in terms of a simpler version of the problem itself.

rules.title: Optional parameters should be passed to "base" calls
rules.desc: When optional parameter values are not passed to base method calls, the value passed in by the caller is ignored. This can cause the function to behave differently than expected, leading to errors and making the code difficult to debug.

rules.title: One-way "OperationContract" methods should have "void" return type
rules.desc: When declaring a Windows Communication Foundation (WCF) OperationContract method as one-way, that service method won’t return any result, not even an underlying empty confirmation message. These are fire-and-forget methods that are useful in event-like communication. Therefore, specifying a return type has no effect and can confuse readers.

rules.title: Methods with "Pure" attribute should return a value
rules.desc: Marking a method with the Pure attribute indicates that the method doesn’t make any visible state changes. Therefore, a Pure method should return a result. Otherwise, it indicates a no-operation call.

rules.title: Empty nullable value should not be accessed
rules.desc: Nullable value types can hold either a value or Nothing.

rules.title: Exception constructors should not throw exceptions
rules.desc: It may be a good idea to raise an exception in a constructor if you’re unable to fully flesh the object in question, but not in an exception constructor. If you do, you’ll interfere with the exception that was originally being thrown. Further, it is highly unlikely that an exception raised in the creation of an exception will be properly handled in the calling code, and the unexpected, unhandled exception will lead to program termination.

rules.title: Cognitive Complexity of methods should not be too high
rules.desc: This rule raises an issue when the code cognitive complexity of a function is above a certain threshold.

rules.title: "ByVal" should not be used
rules.desc: Since Visual Studio 2010 SP1, the ByVal parameter modifier is implicitly applied, and therefore not required anymore. Removing it from your source code will improve readability.

rules.title: "IIf" should not be used
rules.desc: Visual Basic .NET offers a non-short-circuit conditional function, IIf(), which returns either its second or third parameter based on the expression in the first parameter. Using it is slower than using If() because each parameter is unconditionally evaluated. Further, its use can lead to runtime exceptions because IIf always evaluates all three of its arguments.

rules.title: "SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle" should not be called
rules.desc: The SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle method poses significant risks and should be used carefully. This method carries the inherent danger of potentially returning an invalid handle, which can result in resource leaks and security vulnerabilities. Although it is technically possible to utilize this method without encountering issues, doing so correctly requires a high level of expertise. Therefore, it is recommended to avoid using this method altogether.

rules.title: Exception types should be "Public"
rules.desc: The point of having custom exception types is to convey more information than is available in standard types. But custom exception types must be public for that to work.

rules.title: Arrays should not be created for ParamArray parameters
rules.desc: There’s no point in creating an array solely for the purpose of passing it to a ParamArray parameter. Simply pass the elements directly. They will be consolidated into an array automatically.

rules.title: "CoSetProxyBlanket" and "CoInitializeSecurity" should not be used
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: "Thread.Resume" and "Thread.Suspend" should not be used
rules.desc: Thread.Suspend and Thread.Resume can give unpredictable results, and both methods have been deprecated. Indeed, if Thread.Suspend is not used very carefully, a thread can be suspended while holding a lock, thus leading to a deadlock.

rules.title: Value types should implement "IEquatable<T>"
rules.desc: If you’re using a Structure, it is likely because you’re interested in performance. But by failing to implement IEquatable<T> you’re loosing performance when comparisons are made because without IEquatable<T>, boxing and reflection are used to make comparisons.

rules.title: Arguments of public methods should be validated against Nothing
rules.desc: Methods declared as Public, Protected, or Protected Friend can be accessed from other assemblies, which means you should validate parameters to be within the expected constraints. In general, checking against Nothing is recommended in defensive programming.

rules.title: Types should be defined in named namespaces
rules.desc: Types are declared in namespaces in order to prevent name collisions and as a way to organize them into the object hierarchy. Types that are defined outside any named namespace are in a global namespace that cannot be referenced in code.

rules.title: Assemblies should have version information
rules.desc: The AssemblyVersion attribute is used to specify the version number of an assembly. An assembly is a compiled unit of code, which can be marked with a version number by applying the attribute to an assembly’s source code file.

rules.title: All branches in a conditional structure should not have exactly the same implementation
rules.desc: Having all branches of a Select Case or If chain with the same implementation indicates a problem.

rules.title: Deserialization methods should be provided for "OptionalField" members
rules.desc: Fields marked with System.Runtime.Serialization.OptionalFieldAttribute are serialized just like any other field. But such fields are ignored on deserialization, and retain the default values associated with their types. Therefore, deserialization event handlers should be declared to set such fields during the deserialization process.

rules.title: Serialization event handlers should be implemented correctly
rules.desc: Serialization event handlers that don’t have the correct signature will not be called, bypassing augmentations to automated serialization and deserialization events.

rules.title: Calculations should not overflow
rules.desc: Numbers are infinite, but the types that hold them are not. Each numeric type has hard upper and lower bounds. Try to calculate numbers beyond those bounds, and the result will be an OverflowException. When the compilation is configured to remove integer overflow checking, the value will be silently wrapped around from the expected positive value to a negative one, or vice versa.

rules.title: Objects should not be disposed more than once
rules.desc: Disposing an object twice in the same method, either with the Using statement or by calling Dispose directly, is confusing and error-prone. For example, another developer might try to use an already-disposed object, or there can be runtime errors for specific paths in the code.

rules.title: Collection sizes and array length comparisons should make sense
rules.desc: The size of a collection and the length of an array are always greater than or equal to zero. Testing it doesn’t make sense, since the result is always true.

rules.title: Assemblies should be marked as CLS compliant
rules.desc: Assemblies should conform with the Common Language Specification (CLS) in order to be usable across programming languages. To be compliant an assembly has to indicate it with System.CLSCompliantAttribute.

rules.title: Assemblies should explicitly specify COM visibility
rules.desc: Assemblies should explicitly indicate whether they are meant to be COM visible or not. If the ComVisibleAttribute is not present, the default is to make the content of the assembly visible to COM clients.

rules.title: Threads should not lock on objects with weak identity
rules.desc: Objects that can be accessed across application domain boundaries are said to have weak identity. This means that these objects can be considered shared resources outside of the domain, which can be lead to them being accessed or modified by multiple threads or concurrent parts of a program, outside of the domain.

rules.title: Child class fields should not differ from parent class fields only by capitalization
rules.desc: Having a field in a child class with a name that differs from a parent class' field only by capitalization is sure to cause confusion. Such child class fields should be renamed.

rules.title: OS commands should not rely on PATH resolution
rules.desc: Executing an OS command without specifying an absolute or relative path exposes the application to PATH-hijacking attacks.

rules.title: Non-abstract attributes should be sealed
rules.desc: The .NET framework class library provides methods for retrieving custom attributes. Sealing the attribute eliminates the search through the inheritance hierarchy, and can improve performance.

rules.title: Method overloads should be grouped together
rules.desc: For clarity, all overloads of the same method should be grouped together. That lets both users and maintainers quickly understand all the current available options.

rules.title: Duplicate values should not be passed as arguments
rules.desc: There are valid cases for passing a variable multiple times into the same method call, but usually doing so is a mistake, and something else was intended for one of the arguments.

rules.title: Map values should not be replaced unconditionally
rules.desc: Storing a value inside a collection at a given key or index and then unconditionally overwriting it without reading the initial value is a case of a "dead store".

rules.title: Methods should not have identical implementations
rules.desc: Two methods having the same implementation are suspicious. It might be that something else was intended. Or the duplication is intentional, which becomes a maintenance burden.

rules.title: Empty collections should not be accessed or iterated
rules.desc: When a collection is empty, iterating it has no effect. Doing so anyway is likely a bug; either population was accidentally omitted, or the iteration needs to be revised.

rules.title: Classes should implement their "ExportAttribute" interfaces
rules.desc: The Attributed Programming Model, also known as Attribute-oriented programming (@OP), is a programming model used to embed attributes within codes.

rules.title: Null checks should not be combined with "TypeOf Is" operator checks
rules.desc: There’s no need to null test in conjunction with an TypeOf ... Is test. Nothing is not an instance of anything, so a null check is redundant.

rules.title: Windows Forms entry points should be marked with STAThread
rules.desc: When an assembly uses Windows Forms (classes and interfaces from the System.Windows.Forms namespace) its entry point should be marked with the STAThreadAttribute to indicate that the threading model should be "Single-Threaded Apartment" (STA) which is the only one supported by Windows Forms.

rules.title: Extension methods should not extend "Object"
rules.desc: Creating an extension method that extends Object is not recommended because it makes the method available on every type. Extensions should be applied at the most specialized level possible, and that is very unlikely to be Object.

rules.title: "ConstructorArgument" parameters should exist in constructors
rules.desc: When creating a custom Markup Extension that accepts parameters in WPF, the ConstructorArgument markup must be used to identify the discrete properties that match these parameters. However since this is done via a string, the compiler won’t give you any warning in case there are typos.

rules.title: Property procedures should access the expected fields
rules.desc: Properties provide a way to enforce encapsulation by providing property procedures that give controlled access to Private fields. However, in classes with multiple fields, it is not unusual that copy-and-paste is used to quickly create the needed properties, which can result in the wrong field being accessed by the property procedures.

rules.title: "Shared" parts should not be created with "new"
rules.desc: Marking a class with PartCreationPolicy(CreationPolicy.Shared), which is part of Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), means that a single, shared instance of the exported object will be created. Therefore it doesn’t make sense to create new instances using the constructor and it will most likely result in unexpected behaviours.

rules.title: Weak SSL/TLS protocols should not be used
rules.desc: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

rules.title: "PartCreationPolicyAttribute" should be used with "ExportAttribute"
rules.desc: To customize the default behavior for an export in the Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), applying the PartCreationPolicyAttribute is necessary. For the PartCreationPolicyAttribute to be meaningful in the context of an export, the class must also be annotated with the ExportAttribute.

rules.title: Debugging features should not be enabled in production
rules.desc: Development tools and frameworks usually have options to make debugging easier for developers, but these features should never be enabled for applications deployed in production.

rules.title: Exposing HTTP endpoints is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Exposing HTTP endpoints is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: "DebuggerDisplayAttribute" strings should reference existing members
rules.desc: The DebuggerDisplayAttribute is used to determine how an object is displayed in the debugger window.

rules.title: "new Guid()" should not be used
rules.desc: When the syntax new Guid() (i.e. parameterless instantiation) is used, it must be that one of three things is wanted:

rules.title: Calls to delegate's method "BeginInvoke" should be paired with calls to "EndInvoke"
rules.desc: When calling the BeginInvoke method of a delegate, resources are allocated that are only freed up when EndInvoke is called. Failing to pair BeginInvoke with EndInvoke can lead to resource leaks and incomplete asynchronous calls.

rules.title: Non-async "Task/Task<T>" methods should not return null
rules.desc: Returning Nothing from a non-Async Task/Task(Of TResult) procedure will cause a NullReferenceException at runtime if the procedure is awaited. This problem can be avoided by returning Task.CompletedTask or Task.FromResult(Of TResult)(Nothing) respectively.

rules.title: Comments should not be empty
rules.desc: Empty comments, as shown in the example, hurt readability and might indicate an oversight.

rules.title: Executing OS commands is security-sensitive
rules.desc: OS commands are security-sensitive. For example, their use has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Using regular expressions is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Using regular expressions is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Encrypting data is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:vbnet:S5542}, {rule:vbnet:S5547} instead.

rules.title: Weak hashing algorithms should not be used
rules.desc: Using a weak hashing algorithm to protect sensitive data can compromise the security guarantees the hash is meant to provide.

rules.title: Configuring loggers is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Handling files is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Handling files is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Executing XPath expressions is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Executing XPATH expressions is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Using Sockets is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Using command line arguments is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Sending HTTP requests is security-sensitive
rules.desc: Sending HTTP requests is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

rules.title: Reading the Standard Input is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Server certificates should be verified during SSL/TLS connections
rules.desc: This vulnerability makes it possible that an encrypted communication is intercepted.

rules.title: Controlling permissions is security-sensitive
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Expanding archive files should not be done without controlling resource consumption
rules.desc: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

rules.title: Temporary files should not be created in publicly writable directories
rules.desc: Using publicly writable directories such as /tmp to store temporary files exposes an application to race condition vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Insecure temporary file creation methods should not be used
rules.desc: Temporary files are considered insecurely created when the file existence check is performed separately from the actual file creation. Such a situation can occur when creating temporary files using normal file handling functions or when using dedicated temporary file handling functions that are not atomic.

rules.title: Encryption algorithms should be used with secure mode and padding scheme
rules.desc: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

rules.title: Cipher algorithms should be robust
rules.desc: This vulnerability makes it possible that the cleartext of the encrypted message might be recoverable without prior knowledge of the key.

rules.title: JWT should be signed and verified with strong cipher algorithms
rules.desc: This vulnerability allows forging of JSON Web Tokens to impersonate other users.

rules.title: HTTP request content length should be limited
rules.desc: Enforcing a maximum HTTP request content length limits how much data the server must accept per request, which helps control resource use and reduces the risk of denial-of-service attacks.

rules.title: ASP.NET Request Validation should not be disabled
rules.desc: ASP.NET 1.1+ comes with a Request Validation feature that rejects requests containing un-encoded HTML, acting as a first layer of protection against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

rules.title: Types allowed to be deserialized should be restricted
rules.desc: Deserialization is the process of converting serialized data (such as objects or data structures) back into their original form. Types allowed to be unserialized should be strictly controlled.

rules.title: Regular expressions should be syntactically valid
rules.desc: Regular expressions have their own syntax that is understood by regular expression engines. Those engines will throw an exception at runtime if they are given a regular expression that does not conform to that syntax.

rules.title: "Return" statements should be used instead of assigning values to function names
rules.desc: Functions can return values using two different syntaxes. The modern, and correct, way to do it is to use a Return statement. The VB6 way, i.e. old way, is to assign a return value to the function’s name .

rules.title: "Option Strict" should be enabled
rules.desc: There are several compilations options available for Visual Basic source code and Option Strict defines compiler behavior for implicit data type conversions. Specifying Option Strict Off will allow:

rules.title: "Option Explicit" should be enabled
rules.desc: There are several compilations options available for Visual Basic source code and Option Explicit defines compiler behavior for implicit variable declarations. Specifying Option Explicit Off will allow creating a variable by it’s first usage. This behavior can lead to unexpected runtime errors due to typos in variable names.

rules.title: Use a testable date/time provider
rules.desc: One of the principles of a unit test is that it must have full control of the system under test. This is problematic when production code includes calls to static methods, which cannot be changed or controlled. Date/time functions are usually provided by system libraries as static methods.

rules.title: Secrets should not be hard-coded
rules.desc: Hard-coding secrets in source code or binaries makes it easy for attackers to extract sensitive information, especially in distributed or open-source applications. This practice exposes credentials and tokens, increasing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches.

rules.title: Regular expressions should be executed with a timeout
rules.desc: Regular expressions without a timeout can be exploited to cause a Denial-of-Service attack.

rules.title: "ExcludeFromCodeCoverage" attributes should include a justification
rules.desc: The ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is used to exclude portions of code from code coverage reporting. It is a bad practice to retain code that is not covered by unit tests. In .Net 5, the Justification property was added to the ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute as an opportunity to document the rationale for the exclusion. This rule raises an issue when no such justification is given.

rules.title: Avoid using "DateTime.Now" for benchmarking or timing operations
rules.desc: The rule targets the use of DateTime.Now call followed by some arithmetic operation.

rules.title: Always set the "DateTimeKind" when creating new "DateTime" instances
rules.desc: Not knowing the Kind of the DateTime object that an application is using can lead to misunderstandings when displaying or comparing them. Explicitly setting the Kind property helps the application to stay consistent, and its maintainers understand what kind of date is being managed. To achieve this, when instantiating a new DateTime object you should always use a constructor overload that allows you to define the Kind property.

rules.title: Use UTC when recording DateTime instants
rules.desc: You should avoid recording time instants with the use of property DateTime.Now. The property DateTime.Now returns the current date and time expressed in the machine’s local time without containing any timezone-related information (for example, the offset from Coordinated Universal Time). Not having this information means that if you need to display this DateTime object or use it for computations in another machine placed in a different time zone, you won’t be able to reconstruct it in the second machine’s local time without knowing the origin’s offset. This will likely lead to confusion and potential bugs.

rules.title: Use "DateTimeOffset" instead of "DateTime"
rules.desc: This rule recommends using DateTimeOffset instead of DateTime for projects targeting .NET Framework 2.0 or later.

rules.title: Use "TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById" without converting the timezones with "TimezoneConverter"
rules.desc: Since .NET 6 you don’t have to use the TimeZoneConverter library to manually do the conversion between IANA and Windows timezones. The .NET 6.0 introduced new Time Zone enhancements, one being the TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById(string timezone) method now accepts as input both IANA and Windows time zone IDs on any operating system with installed time zone data. TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById will automatically convert its input from IANA to Windows and vice versa if the requested time zone is not found on the system.

rules.title: Use a format provider when parsing date and time
rules.desc: When converting a string representation of a date and time to a DateTime object or any other temporal type with one of the available system parsing methods, you should always provide an IFormatProvider parameter.

rules.title: Don't hardcode the format when turning dates and times to strings
rules.desc: Hardcoding the date and time format strings can lead to formats that consumers misunderstand. Also, if the same format is meant to be used in multiple places, it is easier to make a mistake when it’s hardcoded instead of using a format provided by an IFormatProvider or using one of the standard format strings.

rules.title: Use the "UnixEpoch" field instead of creating "DateTime" instances that point to the beginning of the Unix epoch
rules.desc: With .NET Core the UnixEpoch field was introduced to DateTime and DateTimeOffset types. Using this field clearly states that the intention is to use the beginning of the Unix epoch.

rules.title: "Find" method should be used instead of the "FirstOrDefault" extension
rules.desc: Both the List.Find method and the Enumerable.FirstOrDefault method can be used to locate the first element that meets a specified condition within a collection. However, for List objects, List.Find may offer superior performance compared to Enumerable.FirstOrDefault. While the performance difference might be negligible for small collections, it can become significant for larger collections. This observation also holds true for ImmutableList and arrays.

rules.title: The collection-specific "TrueForAll" method should be used instead of the "All" extension
rules.desc: Both the List.TrueForAll method and the IEnumerable.All method can be used to check if all list elements satisfy a given condition in a collection. However, List.TrueForAll can be faster than IEnumerable.All for List objects. The performance difference may be minor for small collections, but for large collections, it can be noticeable.

rules.title: Collection-specific "Exists" method should be used instead of the "Any" extension
rules.desc: Both the List.Exists method and IEnumerable.Any method can be used to find the first element that satisfies a predicate in a collection. However, List.Exists can be faster than IEnumerable.Any for List objects, as well as requires significantly less memory. For small collections, the performance difference may be negligible, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies to ImmutableList and arrays too.

rules.title: The collection should be filtered before sorting by using "Where" before "OrderBy"
rules.desc: When working with LINQ in C#, it is recommended to pay attention to the order in which methods are chained, especially when using Where and OrderBy methods. It is advised to call the Where method before OrderBy because Where filters the elements of the sequence based on a given condition and returns a new sequence containing only the elements that satisfy that condition. Calling OrderBy before Where, may end up sorting elements that will be later discarded, which can lead to inefficiency. Conversely, calling Where before OrderBy, will first filter the sequence to include only the elements of interest, and then sort them based on the specified order.

rules.title: Prefer indexing instead of "Enumerable" methods on types implementing "IList"
rules.desc: Indexes in C# provide direct access to an element at a specific position within an array or collection. When compared to Enumerable methods, indexing can be more efficient for certain scenarios, such as iterating over a large collection, due to avoiding the overhead of checking the underlying collection type before accessing it.

rules.title: "Min/Max" properties of "Set" types should be used instead of the "Enumerable" extension methods
rules.desc: Both the Enumerable.Max extension method and the SortedSet<T>.Max property can be used to find the maximum value in a SortedSet<T>. However, SortedSet<T>.Max is much faster than Enumerable.Max. For small collections, the performance difference may be minor, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies for the Min property as well.

rules.title: "StartsWith" and "EndsWith" overloads that take a "char" should be used instead of the ones that take a "string"
rules.desc: With string.StartsWith(char) and string.EndsWith(char), only the first character of the string is compared to the provided character, whereas the string versions of those methods have to do checks about the current StringComparison and CultureInfo. Thus, the char overloads are significantly faster for default comparison scenarios.

rules.title: The lambda parameter should be used instead of capturing arguments in "ConcurrentDictionary" methods
rules.desc: When using the ConcurrentDictionary, there are many overloads of the GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate methods that take both a TKey argument and a lambda that expects a TKey parameter. This means that the right side of the lambda can be written using either the lambda’s parameter or the method’s argument. However, using the method’s argument leads to the lambda capturing it, and the compiler will need to generate a class and instantiate it before the call. This means memory allocations, as well as more time spend during Garbage Collection.

rules.title: "First" and "Last" properties of "LinkedList" should be used instead of the "First()" and "Last()" extension methods
rules.desc: Both the Enumerable.First extension method and the LinkedList<T>.First property can be used to find the first value in a LinkedList<T>. However, LinkedList<T>.First is much faster than Enumerable.First. For small collections, the performance difference may be minor, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies for the Last property as well.

rules.title: "Contains" should be used instead of "Any" for simple equality checks
rules.desc: When testing if a collection contains a specific item by simple equality, both ICollection.Contains(T item) and IEnumerable.Any(x ⇒ x == item) can be used. However, Any searches the data structure in a linear manner using a foreach loop, whereas Contains is considerably faster in some collection types, because of the underlying implementation. rules.title: ASP.NET controller actions should not have a route template starting with "/"
rules.desc: Route templates for ASP.NET controller actions, defined via a RouteAttribute or any derivation of HttpMethodAttribute, should not start with "/".

Workaround incomplete diagnostics in Visual Studio 2015 Update 1
rules.desc:
Visual Studio 2015 Update 1 contains a bug which can cause diagnostics to occasionally not display in the Errors window. When this occurs, it is impossible to use the code fixes to address style violations reported during a build. This analyzer works around the bug (dotnet/roslyn#7446).

When this analyzer is enabled, all diagnostics will eventually be reported in the Error window, but the performance of the analyzers is reduced. The rule is disabled for maximum performance, but can be enabled if users notice errors appearing during a build but not while editing, and they wish to use the code fixes to correct them.

Note that some situations are not affected by the bug:

* When building a project, all relevant warnings are reported even if this rule is disabled.
* The various Fix All operations work properly for the selected scope, even if only a subset of the violations are appearing in the Errors window.
